reading.title: Check It Before You Share It
reading.purpose: Weigh an argument for slowing down and checking a claim before passing it on.
paras: Every day, a flood of posts, photos, and videos washes over us, and most of us share a few of them without a second thought. I believe we should slow down. A false claim can travel as fast as a true one, and the person who passes it along becomes part of the problem. Checking takes only a few minutes, and it begins with a simple habit.

First, find the source. Like the source of a river, the place where information begins tells you what you are drinking. Ask who made the post and why. A reputable outlet names its writers, shows its evidence, and fixes its errors in public. A page with no author, no date, and no links is a poor bet, however confident it sounds.

Second, verify the claim. Search for the same story somewhere else, and look at the date and place a photo was taken. A picture that is authentic was really taken where and when its caption says, while a fake may be an old image with a new label. When a claim rests on numbers, find out who ran the survey and how many people answered it. A survey of ten friends cannot speak for a whole city.

Third, decide what is relevant. A true fact can still mislead if it has nothing to do with the question. A chart of summer ice cream sales, for example, says nothing useful about school lunches. When you compile evidence, keep only what connects to your point. When the topic is hard, consult an expert, which means asking someone who knows the field well, such as a librarian, a doctor, or a teacher.

Finally, cite what you use. When you name where a fact came from, readers can check your work, and your own words become easier to trust. An honest inquiry does not stop at the first answer that feels right. It ends with evidence that you can show to someone else. So before you press share, ask whether you have found the source, tested the claim, and kept only what matters. If the answer is yes, share away.

qs.q: In paragraph 3, the word "authentic" most nearly means
choices: shared by a large number of people
really what its caption says it is
old enough to count as history
qs.why: The sentence explains it: an authentic picture "was really taken where and when its caption says," unlike a fake.

qs.q: Which sentence shows what a reputable outlet does?
choices: Ask who made the post and why.
A reputable outlet names its writers, shows its evidence, and fixes its errors in public.
A page with no author, no date, and no links is a poor bet, however confident it sounds.
Like the source of a river, the place where information begins tells you what you are drinking.
qs.why: This sentence lists the habits of a trustworthy outlet: naming writers, showing evidence, and fixing errors openly.

ev.text: A reputable outlet names its writers, shows its evidence, and fixes its errors in public.

qs.q: What is the main idea of this reading?
choices: Only experts, and never ordinary readers, should decide which posts get shared.
Online posts should be avoided altogether because most of them are false.
Surveys are the most trustworthy kind of evidence that a person can find.
People should check a claim's source and evidence before they share it.
qs.why: Each paragraph adds a step for checking information, and the last one tells readers to ask those questions before they press share.

qs.q: Why does the writer say that a survey of ten friends cannot speak for a whole city?
choices: Ten people are too few to show what a whole city thinks.
Friends rarely give honest answers when they are asked questions.
Only a government office is allowed to run a survey in a city.
A survey is useful only when it asks about food or sports.
qs.why: The writer connects a trustworthy number to how many people answered, so a very small group cannot stand for thousands of people.
